summary: Presents the applicability of the Energy Management information model to different scenarios, with use cases and target devices. It helps identify requirements for the energy management framework and MIBs.

eli5.summary: Where might you measure and control how much power gadgets use? Examples of it.

questions: how does poe power reporting work
subtitle: A tour of the places where network-connected devices can report and control their own electricity use.

tldr.problem: Devices on a network use electricity, but metering is often done through proprietary means, which makes the information hard to view across an enterprise.
tldr.mechanism: This applicability statement walks through twelve scenarios, from switches and PoE phones to data centers and printers, and boils them down to a few patterns of metering, supplying and controlling power with the EMAN framework.
tldr.outcome: It gives the EMAN framework and MIBs a set of use cases to be checked against, explains how EMAN relates to other energy standards, and states clearly what EMAN does not cover.

today: RFC 7603 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2015. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata, and it is an applicability statement rather than a protocol specification.

sections.title: What EMAN Is For
sections.content:
The Energy Management (EMAN) framework from RFC 7326 is about monitoring and managing the energy use of energy objects: network equipment and its components, plus devices connected directly or indirectly to the network. It describes how energy information can be fetched from IP-enabled devices using SNMP and MIB modules.

This document describes typical uses of the framework, its opportunities and its limits. It also reviews other standards that overlap EMAN in part but address different domains.

The EMAN document set also includes requirements (RFC 6988), the framework itself, an Energy Object Context MIB (RFC 7461), a Monitoring and Control MIB (RFC 7460) and a Battery MIB (RFC 7577).
sections.eli5: EMAN is a shared way for gadgets on a network to say how much power they use. This paper shows where that could help.

sections.title: Measuring and Managing Energy
sections.content:
Many smart devices already measure their own consumption. Intelligent power strips and some Power over Ethernet (PoE) switches can meter the devices connected to them. When this is reported through proprietary means, though, it is hard to view at the enterprise level. EMAN's main goal is a standard information model that works for end devices, meters and proxies, so a management system can learn who is consuming what, and when.

Because an energy object can both consume and supply energy, the RFC describes three kinds of measurement: energy input to a device, energy supplied to other devices, and net energy consumed, which is the difference between the two.

EMAN also supports control, not just passive monitoring. Control can be as simple as on and off, but often needs context. For example, outside business hours some phones must stay available for emergencies, and office cooling is usually reduced rather than switched off. The power states in the framework can also be used in demand-response scenarios.

A Network Management System that deals only with energy is called an Energy Management System (EnMS). It may only monitor, or it may also control.
sections.eli5: A meter can show how much power a toy uses, and a switch can turn it off. But a smart helper knows some toys, like the emergency phone, must never be switched off.

sections.title: Scenarios for Network and Powered Devices
sections.content:
Section 2 gives a series of scenarios. For each one it lists the target devices, how they are powered and how reporting or control is done.

  • Network infrastructure. Routers and switches and their components such as line cards, processors, fans and ports. The ENTITY-MIB (RFC 6933) provides the containment model that says which energy object sits inside which.
  • Devices powered by a network device. A PoE switch is Power Sourcing Equipment (PSE) and an IP phone is a Powered Device (PD), as in RFC 3621. The switch can switch each port on and off, usually meter the power, and aggregate the consumption of many phones. If the endpoint also supports EMAN, two reporting paths exist, and the implementation decides which to use.
  • Devices connected to a network. A PC that gets data from a switch but power from a wall outlet can report its own usage, or be metered by a Smart PDU through a metered-by relationship.
  • Power meters. PDUs, standalone meters and utility meters measure devices that cannot measure themselves.
  • Mid-level managers. A switch or proxy collects EMAN data from other devices and reports the aggregate to an EnMS or a higher manager.
sections.eli5: A power strip with a meter can tell you how much each plugged-in thing uses. A switch can be the class monitor, collecting everyone's numbers and reporting them together.

sections.title: Buildings, Data Centers and Special Devices
sections.content:
The remaining scenarios cover larger or more specialized settings.

  • Non-residential building gateways. Building management systems often use legacy protocols that are not based on IP. A gateway converts between them and the EMAN framework, talking BACnet, Modbus or ZigBee on one side.
  • Home energy gateways. A proxy that collects consumption from appliances and could apply policies based on time of day, occupancy or utility pricing.
  • Data centers. A hierarchy of servers, top-of-the-rack switches, aggregation switches and core switches, plus UPS units. The RFC notes that there is currently no link between the UPS MIB and the ENTITY MIB.
  • Energy storage. Batteries have finite capacity and lifetime, so charge, age and state need reporting, and an alarm is useful when remaining life falls below a threshold.
  • Industrial automation. The Common Industrial Protocol (CIP) is commonly used for reporting.
  • Printers. They have many low-power modes and use high power for short bursts, so periodic polling of power levels alone would not suffice.
  • Demand response. Real-time monitoring lets an EnMS shut down lower priority devices or reduce power to a class of devices when costs rise or supply falls short.
sections.eli5: The same idea works in a house, an office tower, a giant computer room and even a printer. Each place just needs a helper who speaks its language and translates for the network.

sections.title: Use Case Patterns
sections.content:
Section 3 boils the scenarios down to four groups of patterns for energy objects.

  • Metering: objects that meter themselves, and objects metered by an external device.
  • Metering and control: objects that do not supply power but can meter, or meter and control, other devices.
  • Power supply, metering and control: objects that supply power to others with no metering, with metering, or with metering and control.
  • Multiple power sources: objects with several sources, where metering and control are done by the same source, or metering by one or more sources and control by another.
sections.eli5: Every gadget either measures itself, gets measured by someone else, or hands out power. Some can also flip the switch, and some have more than one plug.

sections.title: Relationship to Other Standards
sections.content:
EMAN leverages existing standards where possible. The RFC reviews many of them and states how each relates.

  • IEC CIM and 61850: EMAN reuses AC power quality measurements from IEC 61850-7-4 and adapts the idea of accuracy classes from ANSI C12.20 and IEC 62053-21 and 62053-22.
  • DMTF: its Power State Management profile covers power-state control but not energy monitoring. EMAN references the DMTF Power Profile and Power State Set.
  • Ecma SDC: defines semantics for data center entities with four power states, and would provide a thin abstraction on top of the more detailed EMAN data model.
  • PWG: its power model and MIB for imaging systems are harmonized with DMTF states. The IETF Printer MIB (RFC 3805) does not address power management.
  • ASHRAE, ANSI/CEA-2047 and ZigBee: building and home information models and a wireless profile. The ASHRAE metering part overlaps largely with EMAN.
  • ISO 50001 and Energy Star: an organizational process standard and a program, neither of which defines how devices report energy.
  • Smart Grid: linked to EMAN through demand response, though EMAN itself does not coordinate with the grid.
sections.eli5: Lots of other groups have made energy rules for their own corner. This section says which ones EMAN borrows from and which ones just sit next to it.

sections.title: Limitations and Security
sections.content:
EMAN does not create a new protocol stack. It defines a data and information model for measuring and reporting energy and other metrics over SNMP, and it considers only limited control capabilities. It does not address Smart Grid questions, electricity producers or distributors.

Because EMAN uses SNMP, it has the security capabilities of SNMP. SNMPv3 (RFC 3411) provides confidentiality, integrity and authentication. Power monitoring and management MIBs may have privacy implications, which RFC 7460 and RFC 7461 mention. This document does not analyze them, and says there may be additional privacy considerations specific to each use case.
sections.eli5: EMAN is not a new postal system. It reuses the one that already exists, along with its locks, and it does not try to run the power company.

items.title: Metering
items.text: Objects that meter themselves or are metered by an external device.

items.title: Metering and control
items.text: Objects that do not supply power but meter, or meter and control, other devices.

items.title: Power supply, metering, control
items.text: Objects that supply power to others, with or without metering and control.

items.title: Multiple power sources
items.text: Metering and control done by the same source, or split between sources.
